summary: DeShawn appreciates Duolingo for its foundational language learning capabilities but finds it insufficient for preparing to teach French in a classroom setting.
top_quotes: Duolingo is like that reliable friend who's always there when you wanna brush up, but it's not quite ready to jump into the classroom with me.
I need deeper dives into cultural nuances and practical conversation, which Duolingo can't always provide.
You know, it's great for picking up vocabulary and simple phrases, but when it comes to creating lesson plans, I need something with more substance.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey there, I'm DeShawn. Nice to meet y'all and happy to share my experiences.

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Well, I grew up in Detroit, and, uh, I've been here most of my life. I'm thirty-five now, teaching high school, which I love. I got into teaching because I've always been passionate about learning and sharing knowledge, you know? Uh, recently, I'm diving into learning French because I wanna offer more diverse language options to my students. It's been a journey, and I'm sure I've got a lot more to learn.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: Detroit, born and raised. The city's got a lot of heart, you know?

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Growing up in Detroit was, uh, pretty mixed. It's a city full of culture and resilience, even when times get tough. The community spirit is strong, and folks here are always looking out for one another, but it also has its challenges, like every big city.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: I'd say deciding to become a teacher was a big turning point for me. I was working in a different field, and, uh, something about it just wasn't fulfilling. I started volunteering at a local youth center and realized how much I love working with kids. That led me to go back to school and get my teaching credentials.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: It was, uh, like I finally found where I belonged. Being able to make a difference in kids' lives every day, it just clicked for me. I knew right then that I wanted to help shape the future, one student at a time.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: I just went all in. Enrolled in education courses, sought mentorship from experienced teachers, and really immersed myself in classroom learning. It wasn't easy, but I was determined to make it work.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, I'm really focused on expanding the language curriculum at our school. You know, giving kids the chance to learn French, which isn't always available. I think it's important for them to be exposed to different cultures and languages.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: It's important because, well, language is like a gateway to understanding. When kids learn other languages, it opens their minds to new cultures and perspectives. I want them to feel like the world's accessible to them, even from our corner of Detroit.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day for me is when a student has an 'aha' moment, you know? Like when something we've been working on finally clicks for them. It feels like all the effort pays off and they're getting it.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: It's those little victories—seeing a smile on a student's face or when they improve their grades. That stuff, it just brings joy to what I do.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I tend to weigh the pros and cons, talk it over with my family and close friends. Their perspectives are valuable to me. I don't rush because I wanna make sure I'm considering all the angles before jumping in.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I'm definitely more of a planner. I like to have things mapped out so I know what's coming. Helps me stay organized and, you know, not overwhelmed.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Well, when I decided to take up learning French, I made a whole schedule for myself—like, dedicating different days of the week for vocabulary, grammar, and conversation practice. It helps me stay on track, even when life gets busy.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I try to be calculated about it. I'll assess the potential outcomes and whether I can handle 'em if things don't go as planned. If the benefits outweigh the risks, I'm more likely to go for it.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: A typical weekday starts early. I'm up around 6 AM, getting ready for school. Once I'm there, it's all about teaching and prepping lessons. I usually stay late to help students and then head home. In the evening, I focus on grading, lesson planning, or studying French.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the classroom time and, uh, the constant engagement with students. It's rewarding but takes a lot out of you. You gotta be on top of your game to keep their attention and, you know, make learning fun.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, I'd like more time to dive deeper into my own learning. I'd love to spend more time developing my French skills or exploring new teaching methods. Uh, there just never seems to be enough hours in the day.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Probably juggling the demands of teaching and personal study. Sometimes, it felt like there weren't enough hours to get everything done, and, uh, it was hard to find that balance.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I try to maximize any free time I get. Even if it's just a few minutes here and there, I use it to review vocabulary or listen to French podcasts. It's about squeezing the most out of what I have.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: I'm real close with my family and a few close friends. They're my support system, always there to listen when I need them and offer, uh, advice when I'm stuck.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: They're like my rocks. We share everything, from struggles to successes. It's a mix of laughter, love, and, uh, just knowing that they're always in my corner.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Most of my time is split between the school and home. Those are my main spots, really.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: I feel motivated when I'm at school, you know? It's lively, and being around students keeps me energized. Home is where I wind down and recharge, so it's calming for me.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: Work is meaningful and engaging, while home is my sanctuary to reflect and relax. Both spaces kinda balance each other out.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: I tend to reach out to my older brother or a couple of close friends. They've always got my back and, uh, usually have some good advice to offer.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: There was this one time when a lesson I planned just didn't resonate with my students. It felt like a total flop, and, uh, I had to step back and reassess my approach. It was tough, feeling like I wasn't getting through.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It was frustrating, made me question if I was doing everything right. But it also pushed me to improve, to find ways to connect better with my students.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I talked to some colleagues, got feedback from them. They helped me brainstorm new ideas and approaches. It was a learning experience, and I took it as a chance to grow, you know?

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking a break to clear my mind works wonders. Sometimes I just listen to music or, uh, go for a walk. It helps me reset and come back with a fresh perspective.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I'd love to be more established in my teaching career, maybe even have a part in shaping curriculum at a higher level. I'd also like to be fluent in French and, you know, be able to teach it confidently in the classroom.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I'd want more time to pursue my own interests, travel a bit more, you know? And I'd like to see the education system evolve to meet the diverse needs of students better.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, I was using textbooks and online resources, mostly. But it was, uh, kind of all over the place. I'd piece things together from different websites, try to practice with whatever limited materials I had. It wasn't very cohesive.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: The worst part was probably the lack of structure. It felt like I was constantly jumping from one thing to another without a clear path. It made it hard to track my progress, and, uh, I often got frustrated.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: There was a time when I realized I had gaps in my understanding, especially with speaking. When I tried to have a conversation, it was clear I knew the words but couldn't string them together properly. It was a major setback, you know.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I think I first heard about it from some of my students, actually. They were using it for Spanish and recommended I try it out. So, I thought, why not give it a shot?

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: I was convinced by how user-friendly it seemed and, uh, the fact that it was laid out in a way that builds on previous knowledge. Plus, the idea of learning a language on my phone whenever I had a spare moment was pretty appealing.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Sure, so, the last time I used Duolingo, I was focusing on the 'Food' module. I started with some exercises that were about matching words to pictures—like, you know, 'pomme' to an image of an apple. Then, it moved into constructing sentences like 'Je mange une pomme.' They had a speaking exercise where I had to repeat a sentence back, which, uh, I always find helpful. It's interactive and keeps you on your toes, but sometimes I feel like I'm just going through the motions without retaining much.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The repetition and interactive exercises, for sure. It reinforces vocabulary and phrases, so you, like, remember them better. Plus, those speaking exercises are really helpful in improving pronunciation.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, it's the lack of real conversation practice. It's repetitive and sometimes feels like it's not preparing me for actual dialogues I'd have in a French-speaking environment. Uh, it's good for drilling, but I need more depth.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: I'd say the lack of context in some exercises. Uh, sometimes it'll ask for translations without much explanation, and it doesn't always cover cultural nuances or slang that are important in real-life conversations.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: There was this one time I was working on, uh, a dialogue section, and the more complex sentences just weren't sticking. I realized that without context, it's hard to really grasp why certain phrases were used. I felt like I was missing out on a deeper understanding.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Definitely. I supplement Duolingo with podcasts and, uh, French films with subtitles. I also try to have conversations with friends who speak French. It's like piecing together a puzzle, you know?

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: Workarounds offer context and, uh, practical usage of the language. They help me see how words and phrases fit into real-world conversations, which is something Duolingo doesn't quite capture on its own.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst-case? I guess it'd be getting to a point where I can't communicate effectively in French after all this effort. That'd be really discouraging, you know? All this work and I can't hold a simple conversation.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it gives me a solid, structured session that helps reinforce what I've learned. Ideally, I’d leave feeling like I’ve actually absorbed something new that I can use, uh, in real life.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: I know it's working when I can recall words and phrases without hesitating and when I can apply them in simple conversations. It's like, when it clicks, you just know.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I'd add more real-life conversation simulations and, uh, cultural context to help users grasp the nuances of a language better. It's about deepening the learning experience.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I'd like to see more integrated platforms that combine various learning tools—like interactive exercises, live conversation partners, and cultural lessons—all in one place. It'd make language learning more holistic, you know?

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: Uh, just wanna say, learning a language opens up so many doors. It's a journey, and having the right tools makes it a lot more fulfilling. Every step counts, even the small ones.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Sure, I mean, as long as it helps improve the learning process, I'm all for it.
